chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Abdullah ibn Aamir, from Ali ibn Mahziyar, from Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Mahziyar, from Quteiba Al-A'sha, who said:

I went to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) to visit a son of his, and I found him at the door; he was worried and sad. So I said, 'May I be sacrificed for you, how is the child?' He said, 'By Allah, he is still with it.' Then he entered and stayed for a while, then came out to us, and his face had turned pale, and the change and sadness had gone.

He said, 'I hoped that the child had recovered, so I said, 'How is the child, may I be sacrificed for you?' He said, 'And he has gone to his Way.' So I said, 'May I be sacrificed for you, you were worried and sad while he was alive, and I saw your state at this time, and he has died in a state other than that. So how is this?'
So he said, 'We, the People of the Household, only panic before the calamity. So when the Command of Allah occurs, we are pleased with its decree and submit to its command.'

key_terms.أَهْلَ الْبَيْتِ: The People of the Household (Ahl al-Bayt)
key_terms.يَجْزَعُ: To panic or show intense anxiety/grief

ai.seo_question: Why did the Imam appear sad before his son died and calm after?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the psychological and spiritual state of the Ahl al-Bayt, distinguishing between pre-emptive anxiety (jaz') regarding potential loss and post-event contentment (rida) with the divine decree. It serves as a practical model for believers, illustrating that deep love for loved ones manifests as sorrow before their passing, while acceptance follows the actualization of God's will. This narrative reinforces the concept of 'sabr jamil' (beautiful patience) by showing that emotional distress does not contradict spiritual submission.
